Q: STM32L433 Precise BusFault on GPIO access (BFAR = 0x48000000) despite enabling GPIO clock A:

I have an l433 board on order, but I already have an l423 and they fall under the same reference manual (register set, enables, etc).

All right the NUCLEO-L433RC-P arrived.

The led is on PB13,so adjust as needed for your board/design (PA5 on your board?). Setting the pin to high turns the led on this nucleo board. (depending on the board design you may need to set the pin low for the led to come ON. Is it sourcing or sinking?).

This works for this board:

void PUT32 ( unsigned int, unsigned int );
unsigned int GET32 ( unsigned int );
void dummy ( unsigned int );

#define RCCBASE 0x40021000
#define RCC_AHB2ENR   (RCCBASE+0x4C)

#define GPIOBBASE 0x48000400
#define GPIOB_MODER     (GPIOBBASE+0x00)
#define GPIOB_OTYPER    (GPIOBBASE+0x04)
#define GPIOB_BSRR      (GPIOBBASE+0x18)

//PB13

int notmain ( void )
{
    unsigned int ra;
    unsigned int rx;

if(0)
{
    PUT32(RCC_AHB2ENR,0x00000002);
    PUT32(GPIOB_MODER,0XA7FFFFFF);
    PUT32(GPIOB_BSRR,1<<13);
}
else
{
    ra=GET32(RCC_AHB2ENR);
    ra|=1<<1; //enable GPIOB
    PUT32(RCC_AHB2ENR,ra);

    ra=GET32(GPIOB_MODER);
    ra&=~(3<<( 13<<1)); //PB13
    ra|= (1<<( 13<<1)); //PB13
    PUT32(GPIOB_MODER,ra);

    for(rx=0;;rx++)
    {
        PUT32(GPIOB_BSRR,((1<<13)<< 0));
        for(ra=0;ra<100000;ra++) dummy(ra);
        PUT32(GPIOB_BSRR,((1<<13)<<16));
        for(ra=0;ra<100000;ra++) dummy(ra);
    }
}
    return(0);
}

But to demonstrate what folks are asking you...

When the peripheral clock is not active, the peripheral registers read or write accesses are not supported.

The enable bit has a synchronization mechanism to create a glitch free clock for the
peripheral. After the enable bit is set, there is a 2 clock cycles delay before the clock be active.

Caution:Just after enabling the clock for a peripheral, software must wait for a delay before accessing the peripheral registers.

flash.ld

MEMORY
{
    rom : ORIGIN = 0x08000000, LENGTH = 0x1000
    ram : ORIGIN = 0x20000000, LENGTH = 0x1000
}
SECTIONS
{
    .text   : { *(.text*)   } > rom
    .rodata : { *(.rodata*) } > rom
    .bss    : { *(.bss*)    } > ram
}

flash.s

.cpu cortex-m0
.thumb

.thumb_func
.global _start
_start:
.word 0x20001000
.word reset
.word hang
.word hang

.thumb_func
reset:

    ldr r0,=0x4002104c
    ldr r1,=0x00000002

    str r1,[r0]

    ldr r2,=0x48000400
    ldr r3,=0xA7FFFFFF
    str r3,[r2]

    ldr r4,=0x00002000
    str r4,[r2,#0x18]

   b hang
.thumb_func
hang:   b .

build

arm-none-eabi-as --warn --fatal-warnings -mcpu=cortex-m4 flash.s -o flash.o
arm-none-eabi-ld -nostdlib  -T flash.ld flash.o -o notmain.elf
arm-none-eabi-objdump -D notmain.elf > notmain.list
arm-none-eabi-objcopy -O binary notmain.elf notmain.bin

On a nucleo board (not saying you have one, but for learning this part, it would be a very good. inexpensive, option) you copy the binary file, notmain.bin in this case to the virtual drive that pops up.

The led simply turns on with the above code. There are instructions between the RCC write and the first GPIO write. (interestingly enough, the last time I tried this on an STM32, the first gpio read worked, even though it should not have, I suspect I know why but...)

Now for the statements in the documentation.

This does NOT work:

    ldr r0,=0x4002104c
    ldr r1,=0x00000002

    ldr r2,=0x48000400
    ldr r3,=0xA7FFFFFF

    str r1,[r0]
    str r3,[r2]

    ldr r4,=0x00002000
    str r4,[r2,#0x18]

Enabling the clock then WRITING to the gpio register on the next instruction. (the two stores being back to back)

Thus the question you were asked, what if you read after writing the rcc register?

This was not adequate, need a longer delay (a read of a peripheral is a pretty good delay):

    ldr r0,=0x4002104c
    ldr r1,=0x00000002

    ldr r2,=0x48000400
    ldr r3,=0xA7FFFFFF

    str r1,[r0]
    ldr r1,[r0]
    str r3,[r2]

    ldr r4,=0x00002000
    str r4,[r2,#0x18]

Two reads was adequate to make it work

    ldr r0,=0x4002104c
    ldr r1,=0x00000002

    ldr r2,=0x48000400
    ldr r3,=0xA7FFFFFF

    str r1,[r0]
    ldr r1,[r0]
    ldr r1,[r0]
    str r3,[r2]

    ldr r4,=0x00002000
    str r4,[r2,#0x18]

Turns out one nop is not enough, two is.

    ldr r0,=0x4002104c
    ldr r1,=0x00000002

    ldr r2,=0x48000400
    ldr r3,=0xA7FFFFFF

    str r1,[r0]
    nop
    nop
    str r3,[r2]

    ldr r4,=0x00002000
    str r4,[r2,#0x18]

Fetches from flash may be dominating the timing. I am running the clock at the default rate so this, relative to the flash and peripherals, is the highest performance.

With a hack/experiment like this I would likely not just leave it at this I would add some margin. Another instruction or two, since the design really does have this limitation. Note that IN GENERAL, there are race conditions and delays required for clock enables for logic blocks, one should always look for or ask the silicon team if there is a delay needed, AS A HABIT...Often a read back is adequate to avoid a race, but...Know how to test, know how to delay, etc. A non-software (silicon) person may say it needs to be x milliseconds, and expect you to go through the trouble of using a timer, where that is not often necessary, its a waste. you can burn predictable amounts of time in other ways. Also understanding when a silicon/hardware person calculates the delay they may be using a worst case situation or like these mcus an assumption about what your clock setup is. (not uncommon mistake for silicon/hardware folks to compute wrong, yet you can figure it out)

The other or lets say a known problem with your code is your delay is dead code, and may be optimized out completely, leaving the loop toggling with no delay

I liked to call this a "glow" the led is not really "on"

    ldr r0,=0x4002104c
    ldr r1,=0x00000002

    ldr r2,=0x48000400
    ldr r3,=0xA7FFFFFF

    str r1,[r0]
    nop
    nop
    str r3,[r2]

    ldr r4,=0x00002000
    ldr r3,=0x20000000

loop:
    str r4,[r2,#0x18]
    str r3,[r2,#0x18]
    b loop

Not as bright but at least with the led on this board it is visible (depends on the led/circuit/physics as to whether you can see the "glow".

It is very possible that using volatile pointers to get at registers, and optimization, I have seen the compiler build the rcc and first gpio writes back to back, which wont work. One version of gcc vs another can produce different code. Same with clang/llvm. Even if you were to, using volatile pointers, do multiple reads after the write, the compiler does not have to generate instructions for those. Volatile does not mean what folks think it mean thus the rant Linus went on about it. Clang definitely has a different interpretation of what volatile means compared to gnu (one should never use volatile pointers to access control registers, in fact there are very few if any use cases for volatile if you want your code to keep working...If your goal is to have the code break every so many years, requiring you to "fix it" (a job security trick) then go for it.)(I have code written 20 years ago that compiles and works today, by not using these bad habits)

SO...

Double check that you are doing the bare minimum at least, enable the gpio clocks in the rcc. Set the moder and otyper as needed, for driving an led, from reset, for this part, otyper defaults to push pull, so you only need to change moder (have to read, CLEAR, and modify the moder bits, you cannot simply set the lsbit).

you need to inspect the binary and see what it is generating, both for the number of instructions between the store to the rcc register and the store to the moder or first gpio register.

Ideally fix your delay loop, having a loop call a dummy function in another compile domain (asm or a separate .c file) is the cleanest (quicky) way to do this and avoid optimization (there are exceptions to that, but...will work for you for now and maybe forever). Volatile may work for the loop variable, but you HAVE to inspect the disassembly to confirm (for each change of compiler, compiler version, or compiler settings

Using a counting loop IS NOT a bad way to blink an led for a sign of life blink an led first program. never start with interrupts, interrupts ALWAYS REQUIRE justification before EVER using them. The first bring up, sign of life program is setting a gpio pin (blinking an led) and one should always do the first program using a delay based on counting a variable to a big number...THEN once you know the led works use the timer in a polling fashion, etc...(in case folks want to say that count based delays are bad).

Note

For read-modify-write with a volatile pointer, one should NOT do this:

These is a bad habits that will bite you some day if you continue, professionally, to write low level code that talks to hardware.

        pGPIOHandle->pGPIOx->MODER &= ~(0x3 << ( pGPIOHandle->GPIO_PinConfig.GPIO_PinNumber));//clearing
        pGPIOHandle->pGPIOx->MODER |= temp;//setting

I do not care if the vendors code does this, mcu vendors libraries have steadily gotten worse over time (if they were ever well written). Professionally, if you choose to go into this profession, your boss wont care if the vendors code is bad, the vendors legal agreement puts all the responsibility on you. You own it...

What is going on here is that you are changing the mode twice. Changing it from alternate function to input and then from input to output (which is what this does) for this peripheral/setting, is not bad. But the HABIT is bad as doing that, on some peripheral, some day, will fail (hopefully not doing damage to the hardware).

temp = pGPIOHandle->pGPIOx->MODER;
temp &= (0x3<<blah)
temp |= (0x01<<blah)
pGPIOHandle->pGPIOx->MODER = temp;

Will keep, hardware, silicon, coworkers, customers and management off your back.

You are on the right track, we need more folks that can actually program hardware, hopefully you read this and try the few things you need to do to get your mcu to work. I really hope you move forward with this and keep trying to write this kind of code.

This one is not horrible, it is still part of the bad habit (s plural). The optimizer will take care of temp = reg ... temp |1... reg = temp. Just look at the code output from the compiler. More lines of c code does not automatically mean more instructions. (good low level programmers know the tools by regularly examining the output).

(volatile uint32_t)0x4002104C |= (1 << 0);

Looks like you are doing the right things. The minimum for this/these parts is enable the clock to the gpio peripheral. Set the output for that pin as output (push-pull), and then start toggling. you will need a delay and if you optimize that code, your delay wont work, but you are claiming you are getting a fault, implying that the gpio peripheral was not enabled.

Here is, not bare minimum as this can be done with less code, but here is some working code for that family, that blinks an led. (bare metal no hal, most any arm-whatever-gcc toolchain, etc)

notmain.c


void PUT32 ( unsigned int, unsigned int );
unsigned int GET32 ( unsigned int );
void dummy ( unsigned int );

#define RCCBASE 0x40021000
#define RCC_AHB2ENR   (RCCBASE+0x4C)

#define GPIOBBASE 0x48000400
#define GPIOB_MODER     (GPIOBBASE+0x00)
#define GPIOB_OTYPER    (GPIOBBASE+0x04)
#define GPIOB_BSRR      (GPIOBBASE+0x18)

//PB2

int notmain ( void )
{
    unsigned int ra;
    unsigned int rx;

    ra=GET32(RCC_AHB2ENR);
    ra|=1<<1; //enable GPIOB
    PUT32(RCC_AHB2ENR,ra);

    ra=GET32(GPIOB_MODER);
    ra&=~(3<<( 3<<1)); //PB3
    ra|= (1<<( 3<<1)); //PB3
    PUT32(GPIOB_MODER,ra);

    for(rx=0;;rx++)
    {
        PUT32(GPIOB_BSRR,((1<<3)<< 0));
        for(ra=0;ra<400000;ra++) dummy(ra);
        PUT32(GPIOB_BSRR,((1<<3)<<16));
        for(ra=0;ra<400000;ra++) dummy(ra);
    }
    return(0);
}

arm-none-eabi-as --warn --fatal-warnings -mcpu=cortex-m4 flash.s -o flash.o

arm-none-eabi-ld -nostdlib  -T flash.ld flash.o notmain.o -o notmain.elf

arm-none-eabi-objdump -D notmain.elf \> notmain.list

arm-none-eabi-objcopy -O binary notmain.elf notmain.bin

arm-linux-gnueabi, arm-none-eabi, etc will work.

for those that complain, in my case I have both a load and function calls between the write to enable the clock and a read of the first register in the gpio (I did an answer on this topic for those/that person, without an abstraction on the write/read, and it was specific to the gnu compiler version and maybe some other factors as to being perfectly unlucky, at the same time, on certain stm32 mcus perhaps, you can read that gpio register, without enabling the clocks, and be fine, as if they fake that read to delay for clock enable)

When the peripheral clock is not active, the peripheral registers read or write accesses are not supported.

The enable bit has a synchronization mechanism to create a glitch free clock for the
peripheral. After the enable bit is set, there is a 2 clock cycles delay before the clock be active.

Caution:Just after enabling the clock for a peripheral, software must wait for a delay before accessing the peripheral registers.

So this one does make this statement/have this requirement.

Please find in your disassembly (arm-whatever-objdump -D myfile.elf) the write to AHB2ENR and the read of the first gpio register. If that str and ldr are back to back you may need one instruction between them. very unlikely that is what you are running into. But I have seen it, demonstrated it. If you are building optimized then lower the optimization level and this will go away, it will likely insert more instructions and cause the delay (if this is even your problem).

What I named as a dummy function dummy(). Is a quick and dirty way to prevent optimization, so calling it in the delay loop simply forces the optimizer to actually generate code to do that count, rather than optimize out delay() as dead code. In this case, if you happen to have this store and load back to back with the compiler you are using, etc, you can use this trick to insert more than a couple of clocks to meet the documentation spec. Or you can use abstraction (volatile pointer stuff, and how they use structs/unions is a very bad practice and should be avoided, there are safer ways to do that without outright abstraction layer)

The volatile pointer stuff combined with optimization, combined with adding or removing lines of code in a function can make timing change (and if super unlucky hit this corner case). As well as the rant Linus did on volatile, also note that llvm and gnu have different opinions on what volatile means and generate code differently, not like you would think volatile means. Can always optimize the abstraction layer to inline without function calls, but when you need to go the other way, cant simply add an abstraction layer, have to re-write everything.

The comment about reading back RCC_AHB2ENR making a difference is the short way to say the same thing (is there a delay). If you add a read after that will be well more than enough of a delay.

        *(volatile uint32_t*)0x4002104C |= (1 << 0);
        x=*(volatile uint32_t*)0x4002104C;
    }

Q: Doctrine ORM "Multiple non-persisted new entities were found through the given association graph:" A:

This problem occurs if you got the related entity in another object manager. For example, if there was previously a check for duplication through an exception and resetting the manager.

Q: PHP on Windows / supported TLS versions? A:

The linked-to question on Expert's Exchange also seems to provide an answer:

it looks like openssl 1.0.1 is needed for TLS 1.2 in PHP, and in WIndows it looks like this is compiled in PHP 5.5 and higher

That matches with my experience of the builds downloaded from windows.php.net, though I haven't done an in-depth test of specific minor versions.

Note that support is based on the version of OpenSSL that PHP (or the PHP curl extension) were built with and is not affected by the libraries used by Windows itself. Therefore running PHP 5.3 (for example) on a version of Windows that supports TLS 1.2 will not give you TLS 1.2 support in PHP.

Obviously, if you were to compile your own version of PHP from source, then the answer would depend on what versions of the OpenSSL and cURL libraries you use when you perform the build, and in that context there is no inherent link between PHP versions and TLS 1.2 support.

However, using the pre-built binaries from windows.php.net, PHP 5.5 is the minimum requirement.
